content:
Applications Actual use in agents and chat Model evaluation Reinforcement learning Why efficiency matters: training is a one-time cost, while inference is repeated many times.
Open-source packages:
vLLM: PagedAttention from Berkeley SGLang: RadixAttention from Berkeley, good for agentic workloads TensorRT-LLM: from NVIDIA Metrics Time to first token (TTFT): how long the user waits before any generation happens (for interactive applications) Latency (seconds/token): how fast tokens appear for one query (for interactive applications) Throughput (tokens/second): how fast tokens appear for many queries (for batch processing) Question: You have to generate sequentially and can’t parallelize over generation, so it’s harder to fully utilize compute.
Review of the Transformer Conventions:
F = 4 D (the MLP up-projects to 4× the model dimension) D = N H (the model dimension is split across N heads) N = K G (for GQA, the heads are split across K groups) S = T (during training, condition on S input tokens to predict T output tokens) Intensity analysis Assuming B is much less than D and F, we can simplify the intensity to B.
If computation intensity > accelerator intensity, we’re compute-bound (good).
If computation intensity < accelerator intensity, we’re memory-bound (bad).
Conclusion: compute-bound iff B > 295.
The extreme case is when the batch size is 1, which happens with inference.
After storing the KV cache in HBM:
Two stages of inference:
Prefill: given a prompt, encode it into vectors (parallelizable as in training). Generation: generate new response tokens (sequential). Unlike MLP intensity, attention intensity has no dependence on B, so batching doesn’t help!
Why?
In MLP layers, every sequence hits the same MLP weights (Wup, Wgate, and Wdown don’t depend on B). In attention layers, every sequence has its own KV cache vectors (Q, K, and V all depend on B). Summary:
Prefill is compute-bound, while generation is memory-bound. Prefill MLP intensity: B × S Prefill attention intensity: S/2 Generation MLP intensity: B (requires concurrent requests) Generation attention intensity: <1 (impossible to improve) Throughput and Latency We know that inference is memory-bound.
Assumption: We can overlap compute and communication perfectly and ignore overhead. In this case, inference time is bound by memory and determined by memory I/O.
# Total memory usage memory = B * kv_cache_size_per_seq + parameter_size # Latency is determined by memory I/O latency = memory / memory_bandwidth # Throughput is the inverse of latency, with B tokens generated in parallel throughput = B / latency Result: even worse latency and even better throughput, though throughput gains diminish too…
When increasing the batch size:
Latency worsens because there’s a larger KV cache (O(B) in size) to read and write. Throughput improves because batching amortizes the cost of reading parameters. Easy parallelism: if you launch M copies of the model, latency stays the same and throughput increases by a factor of M!
Harder parallelism: shard the model and the KV cache.
Use smaller batch sizes during prefill for faster TTFT.
Use larger batch sizes during generation to improve throughput.
How to reduce the KV cache size without hurting efficiency too much GQA reduces the KV cache size by a factor of N/K Multi-head latent attention (MLA) DeepSeek-V2: reduce N × H = 16384 to C = 512.
Wrinkle: MLA is not compatible with RoPE, so we need to add 64 dimensions for RoPE, giving 512 + 64 = 576 total dimensions.
Check the accuracy: MHA is better than GQA.
CLA Share KVs across layers, just as GQA shares KVs across heads.
Sliding window attention I remember MiMo V2.6 used it.
Idea: just look at the local context, which is most relevant for modeling.
The effective context scales linearly with the number of layers.
Problem: this can still hurt accuracy.
Solution: interleave local attention with global attention.
DeepSeek-V4 attention Other ideas Linear attention: Mamba 2, Gated DeltaNet
Quantization # Mechanics x = 5.2342 scale = 0.1 zero_point = 4 x_quant = round(x / scale) + zero_point # Quantize x_approx = (x_quant - zero_point) * scale # Dequantize Post-training quantization (PTQ): Run on sample data to determine the scale and zero point for each layer or tensor.
Quantization-aware training (QAT): During training, quantize and dequantize during the forward pass to simulate quantization errors.
Other methods: activation-aware training and model pruning.
Speculative sampling Checking is faster than generation.
Use a cheaper draft model p to guess a few tokens.
Evaluate them with the target model q (process the tokens in parallel), and accept them if they look good.
Rejection sampling: the key property is that it guarantees an exact sample from the target model!
Medusa: the draft model generates multiple tokens in parallel. EAGLE: the draft model takes high-level features from the target model. There’s lots of room for innovation on the draft model (involves training). Continuous batching & selective batching Inference: requests arrive and finish at different times, so you have a ragged array.
Solution: use iteration-level scheduling to add new requests to the batch as they arrive.
Problem: continuous batching works when all sequences have the same dimensionality, but requests may have different lengths.
Solution: continuous batching.
Attention computation stays the same: process each sequence separately.
Non-attention computation: sequences can be concatenated.
Paged Attention Problem: fragmentation (external and internal).
Solution: paged attention, which also makes sharing easy.
Other vLLM optimizations:
Use a kernel to fuse block reads and attention. Use the latest kernels. Use CUDA graphs to avoid kernel launch overhead.
summary: CS336 notes on inference efficiency, KV caches, quantization, speculative sampling, and batching.
title: Inference by CS336

content:
Building blocks of distributed communication The difference between microbatching and data parallelism is that microbatching distributes batches across the temporal dimension, while data parallelism distributes them across GPUs.
Rank: A particular device/GPU (e.g., 0, 1, 2, 3). World size: The total number of devices (e.g., 4). Operations:
Foundations: Broadcast, gather, and reduce. Workhorse: All-gather (gather to all ranks). Reduce-scatter reduces over dimensions and scatters the results across ranks. All-reduce is reduce-scatter followed by all-gather. The order matters. All-to-all for MoEs is the most general operation. Each rank sends a tensor to every other rank. With balanced splits, it looks like a transpose. Scatter is the inverse of gather. RDMA enables one GPU to directly read from or write to another GPU’s memory without involving the CPU.
InfiniBand supports RDMA. NCCL (NVIDIA Collective Communications Library) translates collective operations into low-level packets sent between GPUs.
Intra-node: NVSwitch and NVLink. Inter-node: InfiniBand and RoCE (RDMA over Converged Ethernet). import torch.multiprocessing as mp # For launching proesses import torch.distributed as dist # For process communication and synchronous dist.barrier # Waits for all processes to get into this point Remember to warm up before benchmarking.
Distributed Training Walk through bare-bones implementations of each strategy on deep MLPs.
Recall that MLPs are the compute bottleneck in Transformers, so this is representative.
Data parallelism Each rank gets a slice of the data.
Data = generate_sample_data
FSDP/ZeRO uses all-gather and reduce-scatter to avoid holding all parameters in memory.
# Only differences between standard training and DDP for param in params: dist.all_reduce(tensor=parram.grad, op=dist.ReduceOp.AVG, async_op=False) Tensor parallelism Tensor parallelism requires very fast interconnects (e.g., NVLink).
Pipeline parallelism local_num_layers Break the batch into microbatches to minimize the bubble. dist.recv dist.send Overlap communication and computation to eliminate pipeline bubbles. Pipeline parallelism can work with slow interconnects, but we need to reduce pipeline bubbles. What we want:
Linear memory scaling. Linear compute scaling. Data parallelism in more detail Naive data parallelism has a memory problem.
FP16 weights for the forward and backward passes. FP32 weights for updates. ZeRO addresses the memory overhead of data parallelism.
Naive All-reduce the gradients.
Stage 1 Split up the optimizer state across GPUs. Each GPU has the full parameters and gradients. Reduce-scatter the gradients, which incurs communication costs. Each machine then updates its parameters using the gradients and optimizer state. Finally, all-gather the parameters, which incurs communication costs. Key finding: ZeRO Stage 1 saves memory for free in the bandwidth-limited regime because all-reduce is equivalent to reduce-scatter followed by all-gather. Stage 2 Split up the gradients and optimizer states. The complication is that we can never instantiate a full gradient vector, but each worker must compute a full gradient because we are using data parallelism. Each worker goes backward through the computation graph incrementally. After computing a layer’s gradients, it immediately reduces them and sends them to the right worker. Each machine updates its parameters using the gradients and optimizer state. All-gather the parameters. Stage 3 Forward: Load the model shard → all-gather the parameters → run the forward pass → free the full weights. Backward: All-gather the parameters → run the local backward pass → reduce-scatter → free the full weights → update the parameters. Two all-gathers and one reduce-scatter. Two important ideas Incremental computation and communication. Overlapping communication and computation. Remember that batch size is a scarce resource ZeRO Stage 3 is nice in principle, but it does not reduce activation memory.
Model parallelism (PP, TP, CP, and EP) splits the work across GPUs but requires them to communicate activations.
Pipeline parallelism processes microbatches Why use pipeline parallelism? It has good communication properties and only sends activations point to point. Batch sizes are key to hiding the bubble. “Zero-bubble” pipelining. Split the backward pass into two parts: (1) backpropagating activations (z, x) and (2) computing weight gradients (W). The second part can be done whenever needed. Tensor parallelism gives each GPU a submatrix Column-wise: QKV and up-projection (no all-reduce needed). Row-wise: Attention output and down-projection (all-reduce needed). On GPUs, use tensor parallelism within a node (up to eight GPUs) because of the high-speed interconnects. Tensor parallelism requires much more communication than pipeline parallelism. Pipeline parallelism uses bsh point-to-point communication per microbatch.
b: Microbatch size. s: Sequence length. h: Hidden dimension. Two all-reduces per layer (attention output and MLP down-projection). BF16 activations use 2bsh bytes. Use tensor parallelism whenever we have low-latency, high-bandwidth interconnects. Expert parallelism EP advantages:
Better GEMM efficiency with larger local matrices, improving GPU utilization. Lower communication. A simpler computation graph makes it easier to overlap communication with computation. Local token permutation is eliminated. DP usually shares replicas with the EP split. DP and TP can interact poorly and lower utilization.
Decouple attention and expert parallelism.
The looped Transformer influenced FSDP.
Use high TP for attention parallelism and low TP for MLP parallelism.
Use ring attention for context parallelism.
See Megatron for more details.
Guideline 1: Minimize Model Parallelism, Maximize Data Parallelism Model parallelism introduces communication overhead that hurts performance.
Guideline 2: Keep EP and TP Communication Within the NVLink Domain EP and TP are communication-intensive. NVLink provides much higher bandwidth than cross-node interconnects.
Guideline 3: Use Pipeline Parallelism (PP) for Multi-Node Scaling Guideline 4: Prefer EP over TP for Expert Layers Guideline 5: Enable Context Parallelism (CP) for Long Sequences A tensor parallelism degree of eight is often optimal.
Activation recomputation enables larger batches, improving throughput.
summary: CS336 notes on distributed communication, data parallelism, ZeRO, and model parallelism.
title: Parallelism by CS336

content:
Programming Model A thread block is a collection of threads that access the same shared memory.
A thread block is scheduled on one SM. There are 32 threads per warp.
All threads within a warp must execute the same instructions in lockstep on an SM. With control divergence, if different threads in a warp need to execute different instructions (if A, else B), the instructions must be executed sequentially (bad).
In Triton, we think from a thread block perspective.
An SM runs multiple warps and switches between them at zero cost.
Warp Occupancy Each thread can use between 0 and 255 registers.
The more registers threads use, the fewer threads can be scheduled on an SM, which means lower occupancy.
Bank Conflicts Shared memory is divided into 32 banks, each 4 bytes wide.
The issue is that in each cycle, each bank can only be accessed by one thread if the threads access different locations.
As a result, if multiple threads access different locations in the same bank, the accesses are serialized (a bank conflict).
In the worst case, consider a matrix where each row spans all banks. Having 32 threads access the first column results in a 32-way bank conflict because each thread accesses bank 0.
Swizzling rearranges shared memory.
Coalescing When the 32 threads in a warp access HBM, memory accesses are combined into transactions of 128 bytes.
In the best case, with full coalescing, all threads access the same cache line.
Block Occupancy Thread blocks are scheduled onto SMs in waves.
The B200 has 148 SMs. If we launch 160 thread blocks, the first wave has 148 blocks and the second wave has 12 blocks.
The second wave has poor occupancy, leaving some SMs idle.
Benchmarking and Profiling Benchmarking measures the wall-clock time it takes to perform an operation.
It only gives you the end-to-end time. Profiling shows where that time is spent.
torch.cuda.synchronize() lets the CPU wait for the GPU.
Use CUDA events for timing.
Triton Specify what each thread does.
The conceptual framework is to load data into shared memory, operate on it, and write it back to global memory.
def triton_gelu(x: Torch.tensor): assert x.is_cuda assert x.is_continguous() # allocate output tensor y = torch.empty_like(x) # determine grid num_elements = x.numel() BLOCK_SIZE = 1024 # number of threads num_blocks = trition.cidv(num_elements, BLOCK_SIZE) # launch the kernal kernel = torch_gelu_kernal[(num_blocks,)](x, y, num_elements, BLOCK_SIZE=BLOCK_SIZE) output_ptx("trition_gelu", kernal) @triton.jit def triton_gelu_kernal(x_ptr, y_ptr, num_elements, BLOCK_SIZE: t1.constexpr): pid = tl.program_id(axis=0) start = pid * BLOCK_SIZE # Indices where this thread block should operate offsets = start + tl.arrange(0, BLOCK_SIZE) mask = offsets < num_elements x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask) # Approx gelu is 0.5 * x * (1 + tanh(sqrt(2/pi) * (x + 0.044715 * x^3))) # Compute (tl.tanh doesn't exist, use tanh(a) = (exp(2a) - 1) / (exp(2a) + 1) a = 0.79788456 * (x + 0.044715 * x * x * x) exp = tl.exp(2 * a) tanh = (exp - 1) / (exp + 1) y = 0.5 * x * (1 + tanh) # Store tl.store(y_ptr + offsets, y, mask=mask) Another Useful Expression block_size = triton.next_power_of_2(N) In the sum example, the row doesn’t fit in a block.
The strategy:
Break up rows into tiles. Each thread iterates over the tiles and accumulates a sum. Perform a final reduction over the accumulators of all threads. The Key Idea of Tiling Recall that each matrix is linearized in memory.
a.stride(0) # a's col num a.stride(1) # a's row num The program ID comes from the grid allocation.
Use tl.arange instead of torch.arange.
tl.dot corresponds to a @ b.
summary: CS336 notes on the GPU programming model, benchmarking and profiling, and Triton.

content:
Floating-Point Formats The idea for bfloat16 originated at Google Brain. Google Cloud’s bfloat16 overview
In 2022, NVIDIA, Arm, and Intel published a specification for the E4M3 and E5M2 FP8 formats. NVIDIA introduced its NVFP4 format for Blackwell in 2025. FP8 specification announcement · NVFP4 introduction
Tensor Operations The following einops examples show matrix multiplication, batched matrix multiplication, reduction, and splitting and merging a head dimension.
from einops import einsum, rearrange, reduce z = einsum(x, y, "seq1 hidden, hidden seq2 -> seq1 seq2") z = einsum(x, y, "batch seq1 hidden, batch hidden seq2 -> batch seq1 seq2") summed = reduce(x, "... hidden -> ...", "sum") split = rearrange(x, "... (heads head_dim) -> ... heads head_dim", heads=2) merged = rearrange(split, "... heads head_dim -> ... (heads head_dim)") Computational Costs A floating-point operation (FLOP) is a basic operation such as addition (x + y) or multiplication (x * y). Multiplying a B × D matrix by a D × K matrix costs approximately 2 × B × D × K FLOPs, counting each multiply and add separately. Achievable FLOP/s depends heavily on the data type.
Model FLOPs utilization (MFU) is the ratio of the achieved model FLOP/s to the hardware’s theoretical peak FLOP/s.
Two quantities help estimate the cost of an operation: accelerator compute throughput and memory bandwidth. Divide the operation’s FLOPs by the compute throughput to estimate compute time. Divide the bytes transferred by the applicable bandwidth to estimate data transfer time.
Accelerator intensity is peak compute throughput divided by peak memory bandwidth. For an H100, this is h100_flop_per_sec / h100_bytes_per_sec. Arithmetic intensity is the number of FLOPs performed per byte transferred by the operation. Comparing these ratios helps identify whether an operation is compute-bound or memory-bound. Large matrix multiplications in training can be compute-bound. Matrix-vector multiplications typically have lower arithmetic intensity and are more likely to be memory-bound.
Backpropagation and Activation Checkpointing For a matrix multiplication, the backward pass computes gradients with respect to both inputs, so it costs about twice as many FLOPs as the forward pass. This estimate applies to the matrix multiplications in MLPs and is also a useful approximation for total model FLOPs at short context lengths.
Activation checkpointing trades memory for computation. It stores selected activations and recomputes the others during the backward pass.
Stanford CS336: Language Modeling from Scratch

content:
This domain requires less compute but more thinking.
Scaling Laws Tricks: Convert a discrete form to a continuous formulation to simplify the analysis. Knowledge: The WSD learning rate mechanism. Dynamics describe how a system evolves over time. Limitation: Transfer across model sizes. Optimization The question is: Why do we still use Adam when there are so many optimizers? Their fundamental starting point is to understand how and why. Intuitively, the magnitude of curvature is proportional to optimization speed. In the quadratic function setting, Adam does not converge. Use a high-precision Python library and set epsilon = 0. In the curvature degradation problem, momentum does not have the expected effect, but Adam does. The loss spike problem. SignGD uses the sign of the gradient without its magnitude. Future: Adaptive Muon. Looped Transformer Goals: Stability and zero-shot hyperparameter transfer. Work in the μP series focuses on dynamics transfer. Loop residual surge. Two parameters: The residual coefficient and the scaling of learning rates. The argument focuses on whether the improvement of the looped Transformer comes from improvements in computation. The metrics are FLOPs, total parameters, and KV cache usage. To make the comparison equal, the width will be reduced, and the experts and attention will be rescheduled. They care about the optimal aspect ratio. The best result occurs with two loops. The scaling law extends to MoE. CE gain measures the benefits of different architectures. With the same loss trajectories during training, the looped Transformer shows its advantage across benchmarks. The gain is more significant in longer, structured text. In-context learning further improves these advantages. DCLM stands for DataComp for Language Models and focuses on the quality of pretraining data. Attention looks the same but reads differently from the baseline. Attention sinks? They accumulate a large amount of attention mass without carrying much important information. Quadratic Model From toy models to universal models. Learning rate schedule. The data mixing problem under a budget. Power spectrum analysis. Mid-training loss is as important as pretraining loss. Hessian spectrum analysis. The quadratic model is not good enough. The edge-of-stability phenomenon. NTK: Neural tangent kernel approximation. Feature loss and kernel loss. Pretraining Beyond a Tiny Language Model Open recipe and open pipeline. Puro’s cost scaling law. Reduce costs. FP8 is another advantage of the RTX 5090’s Blackwell architecture. Muon Hyperball = Muon + projection + effective learning rate control. Multiple power laws. Effective learning rate: Hunyuan’s shift from LR to ELR. The 2022 Chinchilla scaling law by Google. A small learning rate underuses a good idea. Auto-Bidding Two earlier paradigms: Solver-driven methods and learned policies limited by data, such as Decision Transformers. Why not use LLMs in auto-bidding? Some people think LLMs lack numerical precision. How precise should this bidding decision be? The perturbation experiment shows its relative robustness. Discretization and the challenge of sequential decision-making. The harness includes:
The system prompt. The current state. Theoretical guidance through insight injection. Short-term memory (STM) for the three most recent steps. Discussions Why Choose This Direction? Curiosity. Questions about architecture. Diffusion language models did not work, which led to theory. AI safety and adversarial image classifiers led to scaling laws. Scaling is magical. Scaling laws, Lil’Log, model size and data size, and then learning rates. The motivation came from practice. The Gap Between Applications and Theory? A deep understanding can lead to real applications. The key abilities for theoretical research are understanding a good question, possibly from industry, and using scientific reasoning to guide the research. Mathematical skills are less important than before. Agentic mechanisms require larger models, quite large ones.

content:
These notes follow Stanford CS336, Lecture 5 on GPUs and TPUs. TFLOPS measures trillions of floating-point operations per second.
Part 1. GPU Architecture GPUs have many small compute units and devote less hardware to caching and control than CPUs typically do. GPUs are optimized for throughput, while CPUs are optimized for low latency.
Each streaming multiprocessor (SM) contains many streaming processors (SPs). CUDA cores perform scalar operations. Tensor Cores accelerate matrix multiplication and accumulation.
Threads, Blocks, and Warps Threads run the same kernel in parallel, typically on different inputs. Blocks group threads that share a region of memory and can cooperate. Each block runs on one SM, and an SM can host multiple blocks. Warps are groups of 32 consecutively numbered threads that the GPU schedules together. Each thread can access its own registers and the shared memory of its block. Data shared across blocks generally goes through global memory, which is backed by GPU device memory and is slower to access than on-chip storage.
TPUs feature large matrix multiplication units, fast memory, and lightweight control. GPUs are also massively parallel, and the single-instruction, multiple-thread (SIMT) model makes that parallelism straightforward to program. Threads are lightweight, and adding SMs can scale workloads with enough parallel work.
Compute throughput has grown faster than memory bandwidth, so making good use of the memory hierarchy matters for performance.
Part 2. Understanding GPU Performance The Roofline Model Operational intensity is the number of floating-point operations per byte transferred. Throughput is the number of floating-point operations per second. The sloped region on the left is memory-bound. The flat region on the right is compute-bound.
Dense matrix multiplication processes all entries, including zeros. Sparse matrix multiplication can skip work associated with zero entries.
Control Divergence and Lower Precision Control divergence. When threads in a warp take different branches, they may have to execute the paths separately. For suitable operations, a kernel can use an execution mask to control which lanes participate.
Lower precision. Fewer bits per value means fewer bytes to move. Modern GPUs support low-precision and mixed-precision operations.
FP16 and BF16 can be used for matrix multiplication and pointwise operations. Reductions such as sums, softmax, and normalization often use FP32 accumulation even when inputs are in FP16. Adding small values to a large sum can introduce rounding errors. Dynamic range matters for operations such as powers, exponentials, and loss calculations. FP32 and BF16 offer a wider exponent range than FP16. MXFP8 scaling factors use E8M0, with eight exponent bits and zero mantissa bits.
Operator Fusion and Recomputation Operator fusion combines operations in one kernel so intermediate results can stay near the compute units, reducing trips to global memory.
torch.compile can automatically fuse some straightforward operations. Recomputation discards selected activations in the forward pass and regenerates them during the backward pass to save memory.
Memory Coalescing, Tiling, and Scheduling Memory coalescing combines nearby accesses by threads in a warp into fewer memory transactions. In the example below, the threads’ addresses fall within one burst segment.
Tiling divides matrix multiplication into blocks so threads can reuse data. Tile sizes that do not fit the matrix dimensions and poorly aligned accesses can limit performance.
Aligning dimensions to a multiple of 32 can be faster than aligning to a multiple of 16, depending on the kernel and hardware. Grouping and ordering threads to reuse shared memory can also reduce global memory accesses.
Wave quantization occurs when the number of tiles does not line up with the available SMs, leaving some SMs idle in the last wave.
Part 3. FlashAttention The output projection, shown as P_mix, mixes the outputs of the attention heads. Computing all pairs of attention scores has quadratic complexity in sequence length.
FlashAttention tiles the query, key, and value computations and fuses the operations. Its incremental softmax tracks a running maximum and a running normalization sum. When a new tile changes the maximum, the previous sum and output contributions are rescaled so they remain on the same scale. Subtracting the maximum before exponentiation makes softmax numerically stable.
summary: Notes from CS336 on GPU architecture, the roofline model, and the techniques that come together in FlashAttention.

content:
Paper: RollPacker: Taming Long-Tail Rollouts for RL Post-Training with Tail Batching
The Long-Tail Distribution Problem The long-tail distribution of response lengths remains a problem.
Tail Batching A rollout stage may fall short of the number of prompts or responses required to form an effective batch. RollPacker addresses this through speculative execution: it overprovisions requests while selectively retaining only the fastest completions. Perhaps this idea is inspired by speculative decoding.
Systematically excluding long prompts distorts the training sample distribution and may harm model performance. My understanding is that preserving the original sample distribution helps avoid this issue.
During stream execution, gradients for completed responses are computed and buffered, but no updates are applied to the model parameters or optimizer state.
Adaptive Parallelism Short rounds impose greater GPU memory pressure because speculative execution launches more concurrent requests, potentially triggering preemption. Increasing the tensor-parallel (TP) size can mitigate this pressure, but it also introduces communication overhead.
RollPacker profiles memory usage offline and selects the optimal TP configuration online.
To limit cross-node communication, TP groups are confined to a single GPU server.
Reward Scheduler The reward scheduler operates asynchronously. Its optimizations include:
Adjusting sandbox timeouts. Dynamically sharing GPUs for judge models. Most layers of the judge LLM are offloaded to host memory, and their parameters are streamed over PCIe in coordination with activation computation on the GPU. Stream Trainer Some GPUs may become idle when their assigned requests finish early. These rollout GPUs can then be repurposed for training.
A heuristic algorithm decides when to reassign GPUs and which GPUs to reassign. This allows training and rollout to overlap.
To preserve training semantics, the stream trainer adjusts the loss scales and defers gradient updates until streaming concludes.
Topics to Learn Next torch.cuda.Stream DAPO Reference RollPacker: Taming Long-Tail Rollouts for RL Post-Training with Tail Batching.
Figures reproduced from the RollPacker paper are credited to the original authors.
summary: Notes on RollPacker’s approach to long-tail rollouts in synchronous RL: tail batching, adaptive parallelism, reward scheduling, and stream-based training.
title: RollPacker: Proposing a Synchronous Algorithm and Addressing Its Challenges

content:
Paper: PrefixFlow: Training-Time KV Caching for Schedule-Level Prefix Reuse in LLM RL Training
Motivation There has been limited work on prefix reuse during training. The related mechanisms in SGLang and vLLM support forward passes only.
The loss may be computed only over the suffix, but gradients still flow to prefix-side parameters through attention. Repeated prefix computation is a real bottleneck.
Workloads with a high prefix ratio include RAG, multimodal tasks, and long-context QA.
During backpropagation, exchanging the order of summation and matrix multiplication yields an equivalent result.
Disadvantages of Using a Single Computation Graph Prefix and suffix computation have heterogeneous context-parallelism requirements, leaving suffix-heavy ranks on the critical path. Prefix activations cannot be offloaded until the graph has finished executing. Pipeline parallelism requires many microbatches, but one graph per group yields only a few. Reducing computation does not always lead to shorter steps or lower memory usage.
Advantages of Schedule-Level Prefix Reuse Context parallelism can be balanced separately for the prefix and suffix. Prefix activations can be offloaded between phases. Pipeline parallelism can benefit from many microbatches. Suffix forward and backward passes can be scheduled more flexibly. Key Design Phase A: Prefix forward. Phase B: Suffix microbatches. Phase C: Prefix backward. Inject the accumulated gK/gV cache into the retained prefix graph and run one shared prefix backward pass. Offloading Mechanism PrefixFlow keeps the hot cache resident, offloads dormant tensors to a pinned host-memory pool, and asynchronously prefetches them for Phase C. It reinvests the released high-bandwidth memory (HBM) in suffix work.
These optimizations all benefit Phase B: they allow larger suffix waves, longer suffixes, and more expensive transient state to remain resident.
Note that one wave can contain multiple microbatches.
Context Parallelism Under context parallelism (CP), each layer must all-gather the prefix K/V for suffix attention and reduce gK/gV back to the owning prefix shards. Prefetching the all-gathered K/V across layers accelerates this process.
This case is more challenging than those addressed by existing approaches such as DeepSpeed Ulysses and Ring Attention.
In Phase B, balancing prefix and suffix work together is difficult. This is also why reusing the prefix within a single computation graph offers limited improvements.
Solution: Balance CP in Separate Stages For non-attention operators, token-wise work is balanced within a single computation mode. For attention, CP algorithms can be applied independently. Gather prefix K/V as read-only data, then reduce the gradients back to the owning prefix shards. Pipeline Parallelism Switch phases locally within each pipeline stage. Suffix forward passes must wait for the required prefix forward computation to finish, rather than for a global phase barrier.
Expert Parallelism Use Rollout Routing Replay, assuming dropless MoE layers.
Implementation Details Framework: TorchTitan.
Phase A does not expose its live graph directly to Phase B. Instead, it creates detached cached leaves for suffix attention and registers coupling hooks on the live prefix keys and values.
Each Phase-B suffix microbatch step builds a short-lived suffix graph, calls backward without retaining the live prefix graph, and accumulates the resulting coupling gradients in the cached leaves.
Phase B is the main target for torch.compile. Phase-A capture and Phase-C delayed backward rely on autograd.
Experiment Design Parallelism Trajectory alignment under composed parallelism. Phase-B prefetching and balancing. Pipeline-parallel stage-local phase switching. Real RL Loop End-to-end performance in terms of training quality (reward and actor loss) and efficiency. Synchronization also improves because waiting times are shorter. No amplification of drift over the replayed trajectory. Speedup varies with the prefix-to-suffix ratio and whether compilation is enabled. Offloading dormant prefix activations creates memory headroom and enables faster suffix execution. Future Directions Kernel-level reuse and schedule-level reuse are complementary. Tree-structured RL data. Long single sequences. Reference PrefixFlow: Training-Time KV Caching for Schedule-Level Prefix Reuse in LLM RL Training.
Figures reproduced from the PrefixFlow paper are credited to the original authors.
summary: Notes on training-time prefix reuse in PrefixFlow: the three-phase schedule, activation offloading, composed parallelism, and experimental design.

content:
How to design a novel architecture with a novel RL algorithm.
Paper: AReaL: A Large-Scale Asynchronous Reinforcement Learning System for Language Reasoning
Challenges Switching between training and generation. Unequal output lengths. Inconsistent policies and stale data. Synchronous systems reduce the batch size per GPU, leading to memory-I/O-bound execution and poor scalability. System Architecture Interruptible rollout workers belong to the generation stage. The interrupt request is “Update Weights.”
Trainer workers accumulate data until the buffer reaches the batch size.
Rollout controller:
Read data and invoke generation → Send responses to the reward service → Store trajectories and rewards in the buffer → Update the model → Update the workers.
Equipped Algorithm For Staleness η represents the maximum permitted staleness in each training batch. Prioritize older trajectories from the data buffer to form a training batch. The rollout controller tracks both the generated samples N_r and policy version i from the parameter server. Favor a large η. In practice, use the parameters before updating as the proximal policy.
For Better RL Results Compared with PPO:
The outer importance ratio always uses the behavior policy as the denominator. The key choice is the trust-region ratio using the proximal policy. Implementation Details I Should Know CPU work: Rule-based computation and TCP-based data transfer. Separate threads and pipelining: Overlap GPU generation and CPU operations. Asyncio coroutines: Avoid mutually blocking waits in the rollout worker. Batching: A padding-free sequence-packing strategy coupled with a dynamic allocation algorithm. Dynamic Batching Instead of using a fixed batch size for sequences of different lengths, AReaL recombines sequences into batches through a greedy algorithm. Long sequences can cause OOM, while inefficient batching can underutilize memory.
Sequence Packing This is not this paper’s innovation. Concatenation enables padding-free execution with attention isolation.
Evaluation Designs Comprehensive comparisons against state-of-the-art open-source frameworks across model sizes. Strong-scaling analysis with varying compute resources. Ablation studies validating design choices. Baseline: veRL.
Ablation: Decoupled PPO.
Insight Allocating 75% of resources to inference and 25% to training demonstrated higher training throughput.
My Prospect of the Future MoE architecture optimization. More design work around the differences between training and generation. Preliminaries Generation involves autoregressive decoding, which requires efficient KV-cache management and optimized decoding kernels.
Training requires careful orchestration of data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism strategies.
Reference AReaL: A Large-Scale Asynchronous Reinforcement Learning System for Language Reasoning.
The AReaL paper figures reproduced in these notes are credited to the original authors. The PPO-Clip illustration is retained from the original notes.
summary: A second look at RL infrastructure through AReaL: asynchronous generation and training, interruptible rollouts, policy staleness, and implementation details.
title: The Second Glance with Infra: AReaL

content:
Through this paper, I understand the research pipeline in infra, especially in how to design an infrastructure for a specific popular training algorithm, which serves as a solid base for me to explore more in this area. By the way, I know a few professional explanations and code organization in this process.
Paper: HybridFlow: A Flexible and Efficient RLHF Framework
Basic Knowledge DP: Data Parallelism, more model replicas. TP: Tensor Parallelism, divide matrix into little matrices. PP: Pipeline Parallelism, attention for one GPU and MLP for another. Inference: One forward pass. Generation: Multiple forward passes. All-Gather: Collect data from all GPUs and each one then gets a complete copy of data. Reduce-Scatter: Collect and reduce data from all GPUs and then scatter part of reduced data to each GPU. Rank: Distributed process ID. Existing Works’ Shortcomings Single controller avoids complex point-to-point send and receive workflows, boosting more flexibility.
Analysis of RLHF (Take PPO as an Example) Actor training: Computation bound, more TP, more PP, less DP. Generation: GPU memory bound, more DP, less TP, less PP due to no gradient, no backward, no optimizer. Model resharding leads to memory redundancy. Code Realization APIs encapsulate distributed computation and support 3D parallelism, ZeRO, and PyTorch FSDP.
Python decorator: Additional functions without changing the code.
NCCL communication primitives collect and concatenate model parameters in each micro-DP group during the transition between training and generation.
Related Work Analysis DeepSpeed-Colocation: Actor training and generation in the same GPU, model resharding between training and generation. OpenRLHF: Each model placed on separate devices, two copies of generation and training models. NeMo-Aligner: Actor/Ref colocate, Critic-Reward colocate, same model for generation and training. Single controller: Insufficient for large GPU distribution. Multi-controller: Inflexible to implement various RLHF workflows. Key Design Single-controller in inter-node. Multi-controller in intra-node. Hierarchical API Use resource pools to manage GPUs. Configure models with different parallelism and then allocate devices. Asynchronous execution using data futures. 3D-Hybrid Engine Workflow: Switch Between Actor Training and Generation Dg is determined by p, t, pg, dg.
All-gather weights → Load prompts → Generate and all-gather responses → Partition weights → Model update → All-gather weights.
Zero Memory Redundancy All-gather within micro-DP groups enables both efficiency and no redundancy.
Auto Mapping Auto parallel + simulation + double nested loop for best mapping.
Nested loop:
Find best placements for actor, critic, reference, reward. Find best allocation for each group. Experiment Design Compare throughput across three RLHF algorithms. Compare throughput under different model placements, GPU counts, and model sizes. Compare the time of different transitions across GPU counts and model sizes. Break down actor model execution time under different parallelism strategies and model sizes. Design Principles Flexible. Efficient. Simple for users. Avoid a central bottleneck. Reference Guangming Sheng et al. HybridFlow: A Flexible and Efficient RLHF Framework, 2024.

summary: My first exploration of RLHF infrastructure through HybridFlow: controller paradigms, hierarchical APIs, the 3D-HybridEngine, and automatic device mapping.
